statement: In healthy adults in sleep-laboratory studies, drinking alcohol in the hours before bed, compared with the same people on a night without alcohol, reduces REM (dreaming) sleep that night: the first REM period came about 18 minutes later (95% CI 8.8 to 27.1) and REM sleep was about 11 minutes shorter (95% CI 1.8 to 20.8) or 2.8% less of sleep (1.7 to 3.9), and the delay and the loss of REM minutes were larger after more alcohol, in a meta-analysis of 27 mostly crossover studies (Gardiner et al., 2025, journal pre-proof). The prediction intervals include no change, so results varied between studies; 11 of the 27 studies were at high risk of bias, most were small, and nearly all gave alcohol shortly before bed. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In sleep-lab studies, drinking before bed delayed and shortened dream (REM) sleep that night, and more so after more alcohol.
population: Healthy adults aged 18 to 70, mostly young (12 studies men only, 4 women only, 11 mixed), in 27 sleep-laboratory studies published from 1966 to 2022
exposure: A measured amount of alcohol drunk before bed, nearly always shortly before bedtime (study amounts and timings on the study card)
comparator: The same people on a night without alcohol (placebo or no alcohol); separate control groups in two studies
outcome: REM sleep onset latency; REM sleep duration and proportion of the night (polysomnography)
magnitude: REM onset latency +18.0 min (95% CI 8.8 to 27.1; prediction interval -18.8 to 54.8), k = 29 effect sizes, n = 212, p = 0.001, larger with more alcohol (p = 0.024). REM duration -11.3 min (-20.8 to -1.8; prediction interval -37.2 to 14.6), k = 13, n = 96, p = 0.026, larger with more alcohol (p = 0.009). REM proportion -2.8% (-3.9 to -1.7; prediction interval -6.1 to 0.5), k = 32, n = 255, p < 0.001, not detectably moderated by amount (p = 0.424) or timing (p = 0.664).

evidence.extracted: REM sleep onset latency 18.0 min longer after alcohol than in the control condition (95% CI 8.8 to 27.1; prediction interval -18.8 to 54.8; k = 29, n = 212; p = 0.001); the delay grew with dose (meta-regression k = 28, n = 200, p = 0.024) and was not moderated by timing (p = 0.657).

evidence.extracted: Time in bed was standardized in only two of the studies analysed for REM duration and comparable in two; the authors note that a shorter time in bed after drinking could itself reduce REM sleep, which falls mostly in the second half of the night.

risk_of_bias.note: 11 of 27 studies at high risk of bias and 10 with some concerns (fixed order of conditions in 11), time in bed uncontrolled in most, no sensitivity analysis excluding high-risk studies.

inconsistency.note: Prediction intervals for REM onset and REM duration include no effect; part of the variation is explained by dose.

indirectness.note: Healthy adults drinking before bed; the narrow timing (shortly before bed) and laboratory setting are stated in the claim.

imprecision.note: Intervals for the pooled effects exclude no change.

publication_bias.note: Not reported in the main text; a funnel-plot supplement is listed but not read.

grade.reasoning: Controlled crossover experiments start high; downgraded for risk of bias and for inconsistency (wide prediction intervals), giving low. Causal wording (reduces) is used because the comparisons are within-person experiments with alcohol given by the investigators. Status replicated: REM changes were significant in several independent studies. Not upgraded for the dose-response gradient, because evidence that starts high is not upgraded.
